title: Diocletian Divides the Empire
objective: After this level you can explain Diocletian's reforms and the Tetrarchy.
summary: Diocletian ended the crisis in 284 CE with four emperors, smaller provinces and price controls, then retired to his palace at Split.

cards.headline: One emperor wasn’t enough. Diocletian tried four.
cards.body: After half a century of murdered emperors, Diocletian’s fix was bold. If one ruler can’t guard everything, hire more rulers.

cards.headline: Rule of four
cards.body: Diocletian became emperor in 284 CE and ended the half century of crisis. His big idea was the Tetrarchy, “rule of four”: two senior emperors, called Augusti, and two junior ones, called Caesars. With four emperors, one could be near every threatened frontier. The junior Caesars also gave the empire a planned succession. That fixed an old problem: Rome never had a fixed law of succession, so every emperor had to pick his own heir. Now the next emperors were lined up in advance.
cards.callout: Tetrarchy: two Augusti and two Caesars

cards.headline: Smaller pieces, fixed prices
cards.body: Diocletian also split the provinces into smaller units and separated civil from military command, so the man running a province was no longer the man leading its troops. Then he took on inflation. In 301 CE his Edict on Maximum Prices tried to stop it by fixing prices by law. It failed. It turns out you can’t order a price to stay put.

cards.fact: Diocletian did what no emperor had done: he retired.
cards.context: In 305 CE he stepped down voluntarily, the first Roman emperor to do so, and moved to his palace at Split, in modern Croatia. After an age when most emperors left office by being killed, this one simply packed up and left.
